sentence: What is the problem with the proposed paraphrase?
setupText: A test summary says, 'The revised model is not more robust than its predecessor.' An editor proposes 'The revised model is less robust.'
taskText: What is the problem with the proposed paraphrase?
text: A test summary says, 'The revised model is not more robust than its predecessor.' An editor proposes 'The revised model is less robust.' What is the problem with the proposed paraphrase?
options: It replaces a comparison of reliability with a comparison of size.
It makes the predecessor less robust than the revised model.
It excludes equal robustness, which the original still permits.
It weakens a definite decline into an uncertain improvement.
answer: It excludes equal robustness, which the original still permits.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-801:Not more versus less and equality-compatible negation
explanation: Not more robust denies a positive advantage; the revised model could be equally robust or less robust. Less robust asserts the lower ranking.

rationales.It excludes equal robustness, which the: Not more robust denies a positive advantage; the revised model could be equally robust or less robust. Less robust asserts the lower ranking.
rationales.It replaces a comparison of reliability: Both sentences retain robustness as their dimension; the change concerns negation and ordering.
rationales.It makes the predecessor less robust tha: Less robust still assigns the lower position to the revised model, not the predecessor.
rationales.It weakens a definite decline into an un: The original does not assert a definite decline; the edit adds one.

sentence: Which summary preserves the stated basis of preference?
setupText: A privacy assessment concludes, 'Proposal B is preferable to A on privacy grounds, though A is cheaper and easier to implement.'
taskText: Which summary preserves the stated basis of preference?
text: A privacy assessment concludes, 'Proposal B is preferable to A on privacy grounds, though A is cheaper and easier to implement.' Which summary preserves the stated basis of preference?
options: B is preferable overall because privacy automatically outweighs the other criteria.
A ranks above B for privacy because it is easier to implement.
B ranks above A for privacy; the sentence leaves the overall choice open.
The proposals are equally preferable once all three criteria are considered.
answer: B ranks above A for privacy; the sentence leaves the overall choice open.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-802:A preference restricted to one criterion
explanation: On privacy grounds limits the ranking to a criterion, while the other advantages prevent an automatic overall conclusion.

rationales.B is preferable overall because privacy: The assessment states a privacy-based preference, not a rule assigning decisive weight to privacy.
rationales.B ranks above A for privacy; the sentenc: On privacy grounds limits the ranking to a criterion, while the other advantages prevent an automatic overall conclusion.
rationales.A ranks above B for privacy because it i: Ease of implementation is assigned to A, but the privacy preference is explicitly assigned to B.
rationales.The proposals are equally preferable onc: The sentence supplies no weights or combined score that would establish an overall tie.

sentence: Which comparison is expressed without adding information?
setupText: A reviewer writes, 'This application is more likely to be deferred than rejected.'
taskText: Which comparison is expressed without adding information?
text: A reviewer writes, 'This application is more likely to be deferred than rejected.' Which comparison is expressed without adding information?
options: This application is more likely to be deferred than the previous application was.
For this application, deferral is judged more probable than rejection.
Deferral is judged more probable than all the other possible outcomes combined.
The application will probably be deferred rather than approved.
answer: For this application, deferral is judged more probable than rejection.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-803:Comparing probabilities of two specified outcomes
explanation: More likely scopes over two outcomes of the same application: being deferred and being rejected.

rationales.This application is more likely to be de: The than phrase compares outcomes for this application, not different applications.
rationales.Deferral is judged more probable than al: Only rejection is the stated alternative; approval and other outcomes are not included in the comparison.
rationales.For this application, deferral is judged: More likely scopes over two outcomes of the same application: being deferred and being rejected.
rationales.The application will probably be deferre: The sentence neither compares deferral with approval nor necessarily puts deferral above a 50% probability.

sentence: Which interpretation best fits the review?
setupText: A reviewer says, 'The speech was more confident than convincing; several key objections went unanswered.'
taskText: Which interpretation best fits the review?
text: A reviewer says, 'The speech was more confident than convincing; several key objections went unanswered.' Which interpretation best fits the review?
options: The speech was more convincing than the speaker's earlier speeches.
Confidence is a better description of the speech than persuasiveness is.
The speaker's confidence caused the audience to accept the argument.
The speech contained a greater number of confident claims than persuasive examples.
answer: Confidence is a better description of the speech than persuasiveness is.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-804:Comparing two characterizations of one entity
explanation: More confident than convincing contrasts characterizations of the same speech; the remaining objections support the distinction.

rationales.The speech was more convincing than the: No earlier speech is the comparison standard; two qualities of this speech are contrasted.
rationales.The speaker's confidence caused the audi: The unanswered objections and contrast with convincing do not support successful persuasion.
rationales.The speech contained a greater number of: The phrase grades the fit of two descriptions rather than explicitly counting claims and examples.
rationales.Confidence is a better description of th: More confident than convincing contrasts characterizations of the same speech; the remaining objections support the distinction.

sentence: Which report sentence preserves both the measured comparison and the limit of the tests?
setupText: Tests show a small robustness advantage for Model B over Model A, but neither has been checked against the required standard.
taskText: Which report sentence preserves both the measured comparison and the limit of the tests?
text: Tests show a small robustness advantage for Model B over Model A, but neither has been checked against the required standard. Which report sentence preserves both the measured comparison and the limit of the tests?
options: B is marginally more robust than A; compliance with the standard remains untested.
B is robust enough to meet the standard, though only marginally more robust than A.
B is no more robust than A, and compliance with the standard remains untested.
B is substantially more robust than A, although compliance remains untested.
answer: B is marginally more robust than A; compliance with the standard remains untested.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-805:A marginal relative advantage versus an absolute threshold
explanation: Marginally states the small relative advantage, while the second clause avoids claiming an untested absolute threshold.

rationales.B is marginally more robust than A; comp: Marginally states the small relative advantage, while the second clause avoids claiming an untested absolute threshold.
rationales.B is robust enough to meet the standard,: The threshold claim is unsupported because neither model was checked against that standard.
rationales.B is no more robust than A, and complian: No more removes the measured positive advantage.
rationales.B is substantially more robust than A, a: Substantially overstates the small advantage established by the tests.

sentence: Which comparison distinguishes the supporter count from the support rate?
setupText: Of 100 residents surveyed in East Ward, 60 support the plan. Of 200 in West Ward, 80 support it.
taskText: Which comparison distinguishes the supporter count from the support rate?
text: Of 100 residents surveyed in East Ward, 60 support the plan. Of 200 in West Ward, 80 support it. Which comparison distinguishes the supporter count from the support rate?
options: East has more supporters in the sample and a higher proportion supporting the plan.
West has fewer supporters in the sample but a higher proportion supporting the plan.
The wards have equal support because both have a majority opposed.
East has fewer supporters in the sample but a higher proportion supporting the plan.
answer: East has fewer supporters in the sample but a higher proportion supporting the plan.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-806:Comparing raw counts and proportions with different denominators
explanation: The raw count is 60 versus 80, while the rates are 60% versus 40%; the two rankings go in opposite directions.

rationales.East has more supporters in the sample a: East has the higher rate, but sixty supporters is fewer than eighty.
rationales.East has fewer supporters in the sample: The raw count is 60 versus 80, while the rates are 60% versus 40%; the two rankings go in opposite directions.
rationales.West has fewer supporters in the sample: Both claims are reversed: West has more supporters but the lower rate.
rationales.The wards have equal support because bot: East has a supporting majority of 60%; neither equal rates nor two opposing majorities follows.

sentence: Which response meaning is best supported?
setupText: A: 'The landlord has offered us one evening with a portable heater.' B: 'Well, it's better than nothing.'
taskText: Which response meaning is best supported?
text: A: 'The landlord has offered us one evening with a portable heater.' B: 'Well, it's better than nothing.' Which response meaning is best supported?
options: B regards the offer as the best option among the landlord's available solutions.
B acknowledges limited value without presenting the offer as satisfactory.
B considers the offer equivalent to receiving no help.
B rejects the offer as worse than managing without a heater.
answer: B acknowledges limited value without presenting the offer as satisfactory.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-807:A low comparative benchmark producing faint praise
explanation: The low comparison point provides qualified acceptance: some help is better than none, but that is restrained praise.

rationales.B regards the offer as the best option a: The benchmark is nothing, not a comparison with all solutions the landlord could offer.
rationales.B considers the offer equivalent to rece: Better than nothing grants some improvement over no help rather than complete equivalence.
rationales.B acknowledges limited value without pre: The low comparison point provides qualified acceptance: some help is better than none, but that is restrained praise.
rationales.B rejects the offer as worse than managi: That reverses the direction of better than nothing.

sentence: What stance does 'as few as' communicate here?
setupText: The organiser writes, 'As few as six people came to the public session.'
taskText: What stance does 'as few as' communicate here?
text: The organiser writes, 'As few as six people came to the public session.' What stance does 'as few as' communicate here?
options: The attendance is given only as a maximum of six.
Six is described as the minimum attendance required to hold the session.
Six people came in addition to the usual attendees.
The attendance is presented as notably low.
answer: The attendance is presented as notably low.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-808:As few as emphasizing a low count
explanation: 'As few as' frames six as a surprisingly or notably small count in context.

rationales.The attendance is given only as a maximu: 'As few as' highlights the low figure; 'at most six' would state only an upper bound.
rationales.The attendance is presented as notably l: 'As few as' frames six as a surprisingly or notably small count in context.
rationales.Six is described as the minimum attendan: The sentence reports turnout; it does not establish a procedural minimum.
rationales.Six people came in addition to the usual: 'As few as' modifies the reported total, not an added subgroup.

sentence: Which reading best captures the curator's emphasis?
setupText: A museum curator says, 'No fewer than forty volunteers helped to catalogue the collection.'
taskText: Which reading best captures the curator's emphasis?
text: A museum curator says, 'No fewer than forty volunteers helped to catalogue the collection.' Which reading best captures the curator's emphasis?
options: The curator presents the volunteer count as impressively large.
The curator complains that there were fewer than forty volunteers.
The curator sets forty as the maximum number allowed to help.
The curator says exactly forty volunteers were needed before work could start.
answer: The curator presents the volunteer count as impressively large.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-809:No fewer than as emphatic quantity framing
explanation: No fewer than highlights the scale of the count, presenting forty as noteworthy rather than merely listing it.

rationales.The curator complains that there were fe: No fewer than negates a lower count rather than asserting one.
rationales.The curator sets forty as the maximum nu: The sentence reports participation; no fewer than is not a maximum restriction.
rationales.The curator presents the volunteer count: No fewer than highlights the scale of the count, presenting forty as noteworthy rather than merely listing it.
rationales.The curator says exactly forty volunteer: Participation is reported, but no minimum staffing rule or start condition is stated.

sentence: Which paraphrase retains B's comparative judgment?
setupText: A: 'Does the second draft come close to the first in clarity?' B: 'It's nothing like as clear.'
taskText: Which paraphrase retains B's comparative judgment?
text: A: 'Does the second draft come close to the first in clarity?' B: 'It's nothing like as clear.' Which paraphrase retains B's comparative judgment?
options: The second draft is clearer but written in a different style.
The second draft is almost as clear as the first.
The second draft falls well short of the first in clarity.
The drafts differ in subject, so clarity cannot be compared.
answer: The second draft falls well short of the first in clarity.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-810:Nothing like as ... as strongly denying approximate equality
explanation: Nothing like as ... as strongly denies closeness to the comparison standard.

rationales.The second draft is clearer but written: Nothing like as clear rejects comparable clarity, not merely similarity of style.
rationales.The second draft is almost as clear as t: Almost as clear understates the large shortfall conveyed by nothing like.
rationales.The drafts differ in subject, so clarity: B does compare clarity; no difference in subject is stated.
rationales.The second draft falls well short of the: Nothing like as ... as strongly denies closeness to the comparison standard.

sentence: What does the edit incorrectly add?
setupText: Across the test sample, Method A was faster on average than Method B. An editor writes, 'A was faster for every participant.'
taskText: What does the edit incorrectly add?
text: Across the test sample, Method A was faster on average than Method B. An editor writes, 'A was faster for every participant.' What does the edit incorrectly add?
options: A comparison with a method that was not tested.
A claim that B has the lower average completion time.
A participant-by-participant advantage that an average comparison does not establish.
A statement that the methods had equal sample sizes.
answer: A participant-by-participant advantage that an average comparison does not establish.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-811:Average comparative advantage versus universal individual advantage
explanation: An average can be lower even when some individual results favor B; 'every participant' is a stronger, distributive claim.

rationales.A participant-by-participant advantage t: An average can be lower even when some individual results favor B; 'every participant' is a stronger, distributive claim.
rationales.A comparison with a method that was not: Both sentences compare A with B; the edit changes how broadly the advantage applies.
rationales.A claim that B has the lower average com: The edit does not reverse the named winner; it overextends that winner's advantage.
rationales.A statement that the methods had equal s: Every participant does not itself report or compare the sample sizes.

sentence: Which assessment is expressed?
setupText: The minutes say, 'Keeping the old timetable would have been no worse than adopting this one.'
taskText: Which assessment is expressed?
text: The minutes say, 'Keeping the old timetable would have been no worse than adopting this one.' Which assessment is expressed?
options: The rejected option is judged strictly better than the adopted one.
The two timetables are said to have produced identical observed outcomes.
The adopted timetable is judged better because the other was rejected.
The rejected option is judged at least equal to the adopted one, not necessarily better.
answer: The rejected option is judged at least equal to the adopted one, not necessarily better.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-812:No worse in an unrealized-alternative comparison
explanation: No worse denies that keeping the old timetable would rank below the actual choice, while allowing a tie.

rationales.The rejected option is judged strictly b: No worse permits equality; it does not require an advantage.
rationales.The rejected option is judged at least e: No worse denies that keeping the old timetable would rank below the actual choice, while allowing a tie.
rationales.The two timetables are said to have prod: Would have been evaluates an unrealized alternative, not two observed outcomes.
rationales.The adopted timetable is judged better b: The comparative judgment points the other way: rejection does not establish inferiority.

sentence: Which requirement does the comparison impose?
setupText: A design brief says, 'The registration process should be no more intrusive than necessary for confirming membership.'
taskText: Which requirement does the comparison impose?
text: A design brief says, 'The registration process should be no more intrusive than necessary for confirming membership.' Which requirement does the comparison impose?
options: The process should collect exactly the same data as the current process.
Intrusion should not exceed what the stated membership check requires.
The process should be less intrusive than every available alternative.
Any information that might later be useful should be collected.
answer: Intrusion should not exceed what the stated membership check requires.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-813:A necessity threshold as a comparative ceiling
explanation: No more ... than caps the degree at a purpose-specific necessity threshold, allowing less if the purpose can still be met.

rationales.The process should collect exactly the s: 'Necessary for confirming membership' is the benchmark, not the existing process.
rationales.The process should be less intrusive tha: The sentence sets a necessity-based ceiling; it does not rank every design.
rationales.Intrusion should not exceed what the sta: No more ... than caps the degree at a purpose-specific necessity threshold, allowing less if the purpose can still be met.
rationales.Any information that might later be usef: Possible future usefulness is broader than what is necessary for the named membership check.

sentence: Which revision removes the ambiguity while preserving that meaning?
setupText: A draft says, 'Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam.' The writer means that Ravi's trust in Lena exceeds Sam's trust in Lena.
taskText: Which revision removes the ambiguity while preserving that meaning?
text: A draft says, 'Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam.' The writer means that Ravi's trust in Lena exceeds Sam's trust in Lena. Which revision removes the ambiguity while preserving that meaning?
options: Ravi trusts Lena more than he trusts Sam.
Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam trusts Ravi.
Ravi is trusted by Lena more than Sam is.
Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam does.
answer: Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam does.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-814:Disambiguating subject versus object comparison after than
explanation: 'Does' restores 'trusts Lena' after 'Sam', making Sam the second subject rather than a second object of Ravi's trust.

rationales.Ravi trusts Lena more than he trusts Sam: This compares Ravi's trust in two different people, not two people's trust in Lena.
rationales.Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam trusts Ra: This changes the recipient of Sam's trust from Lena to Ravi.
rationales.Ravi is trusted by Lena more than Sam is: This makes Lena the trusting person and compares her trust in Ravi and Sam.
'Does' restores 'trusts Lena' after 'Sam', making Sam the second subject rather than a second object of Ravi's trust.

sentence: Which comparison does the review make, without adding a historical claim?
setupText: A review says, 'The archive is less accessible than it could be.'
taskText: Which comparison does the review make, without adding a historical claim?
text: A review says, 'The archive is less accessible than it could be.' Which comparison does the review make, without adding a historical claim?
options: Current accessibility is lower than it was before the refurbishment.
Current accessibility is below that of every similar archive.
Current accessibility has fallen even though no improvement is possible.
Current accessibility is below an attainable level.
answer: Current accessibility is below an attainable level.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-815:Potential degree as the standard of comparison
explanation: Could be supplies a possible improved state as the standard, not a claim about the archive's past.

rationales.Current accessibility is below an attain: Could be supplies a possible improved state as the standard, not a claim about the archive's past.
rationales.Current accessibility is lower than it w: No earlier state or refurbishment is named in the sentence.
rationales.Current accessibility is below that of e: The comparison is with the archive's own potential, not a complete set of other archives.
rationales.Current accessibility has fallen even th: The sentence neither asserts a decline over time nor denies possible improvement.

sentence: Which claim preserves the report's ranking and comparison set?
setupText: A salary report calls Noor 'the highest-paid part-time employee in the department,' using annual earnings before tax.
taskText: Which claim preserves the report's ranking and comparison set?
text: A salary report calls Noor 'the highest-paid part-time employee in the department,' using annual earnings before tax. Which claim preserves the report's ranking and comparison set?
options: Noor earns more per hour than any employee in the department.
Noor's annual earnings exceed those of all full-time departmental staff.
No other part-time departmental employee has higher annual earnings before tax.
Noor is the department's only part-time employee at that annual earnings level.
answer: No other part-time departmental employee has higher annual earnings before tax.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-816:A superlative restricted by employment category and measurement basis
explanation: This retains the subgroup and annual measure without inventing an hourly ranking or excluding possible ties.

rationales.Noor earns more per hour than any employ: 'Hourly pay' is a different measure, and 'any employee' expands the group beyond part-time staff.
rationales.No other part-time departmental employee: This retains the subgroup and annual measure without inventing an hourly ranking or excluding possible ties.
rationales.Noor's annual earnings exceed those of a: Full-time staff are outside the stated comparison group.
rationales.Noor is the department's only part-time: Highest-paid does not by itself exclude another employee tied at the same level.

sentence: Which sentence meets that precise reporting goal?
setupText: Approval rose from 40% to 50%. The report must describe the increase in percentage points, not the relative percentage increase.
taskText: Which sentence meets that precise reporting goal?
text: Approval rose from 40% to 50%. The report must describe the increase in percentage points, not the relative percentage increase. Which sentence meets that precise reporting goal?
options: Approval was ten percentage points higher than before.
Approval was ten percent higher than before.
Approval was twenty-five percentage points higher than before.
Approval was fifty percentage points higher than before.
answer: Approval was ten percentage points higher than before.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-817:Percentage-point difference versus relative percentage increase
explanation: Percentage points compare the displayed percentages directly: fifty minus forty is ten points.

rationales.Approval was ten percent higher than bef: A ten-percent relative increase on forty would reach forty-four; the required measure is percentage points.
rationales.Approval was twenty-five percentage poin: Twenty-five is the relative percentage increase, not the point difference between forty and fifty.
rationales.Approval was ten percentage points highe: Percentage points compare the displayed percentages directly: fifty minus forty is ten points.
rationales.Approval was fifty percentage points hig: Fifty is the new rate, not its increase over forty.

sentence: What does B's comparative expression convey?
setupText: A: 'Did the second briefing explain why the venue changed?' B: 'I'm none the wiser.'
taskText: What does B's comparative expression convey?
text: A: 'Did the second briefing explain why the venue changed?' B: 'I'm none the wiser.' What does B's comparative expression convey?
options: B now understands the reason but disagrees with the decision.
The briefing has not improved B's understanding of the reason.
B knows less about the reason than before the briefing.
B understands less than every other person at the briefing.
answer: The briefing has not improved B's understanding of the reason.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-818:None the wiser as a negative result comparison
explanation: 'None the wiser' means no better informed as a result of the intervening event.

rationales.B now understands the reason but disagre: None the wiser denies a gain in understanding; disagreement is not the stated issue.
rationales.B knows less about the reason than befor: The idiom signals no improvement, not necessarily an actual loss of knowledge.
rationales.B understands less than every other pers: The comparison concerns B's change in understanding, not a ranking of participants.
rationales.The briefing has not improved B's unders: 'None the wiser' means no better informed as a result of the intervening event.

sentence: Which reading best fits B's reply?
setupText: A: 'Has the extension been approved?' B: 'It's as good as approved; only the routine signature is missing.'
taskText: Which reading best fits B's reply?
text: A: 'Has the extension been approved?' B: 'It's as good as approved; only the routine signature is missing.' Which reading best fits B's reply?
options: B treats approval as virtually settled while acknowledging it is not formally complete.
B compares the quality of this approval with that of an earlier approval.
B says approval and rejection remain equally likely.
B confirms that every required approval step has been completed.
answer: B treats approval as virtually settled while acknowledging it is not formally complete.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-819:As good as before a participle expressing virtual completion
explanation: 'As good as approved' means effectively or almost approved here; the missing signature keeps formal completion separate.

rationales.B treats approval as virtually settled w: 'As good as approved' means effectively or almost approved here; the missing signature keeps formal completion separate.
rationales.B compares the quality of this approval: As good as before approved has a near-equivalence meaning, not a quality ranking between approvals.
rationales.B says approval and rejection remain equ: 'As good as approved' expresses strong expectation of approval, not an evenly balanced outcome.
rationales.B confirms that every required approval: The routine signature is explicitly still missing, so formal completion is not claimed.

sentence: Which paraphrase preserves the units being compared?
setupText: An exhibition review says, 'No single photograph is more powerful than the sequence as a whole.'
taskText: Which paraphrase preserves the units being compared?
text: An exhibition review says, 'No single photograph is more powerful than the sequence as a whole.' Which paraphrase preserves the units being compared?
options: The complete sequence is at least as powerful as each individual photograph.
Each photograph is equally powerful when displayed by itself.
The complete sequence is more powerful than all photographs outside the exhibition.
The sequence's power is exactly the sum of the individual photographs' power.
answer: The complete sequence is at least as powerful as each individual photograph.
focusKey: coverage-comparatives-c1-820:Comparing a whole with each part under a negative universal
explanation: No individual image exceeds the whole; at least as powerful preserves possible equality as well as superiority of the whole.

rationales.Each photograph is equally powerful when: The sentence compares each photograph with the whole, not individual photographs with one another.
rationales.The complete sequence is at least as pow: No individual image exceeds the whole; at least as powerful preserves possible equality as well as superiority of the whole.
rationales.The complete sequence is more powerful t: The comparison does not extend to photographs outside this sequence.
rationales.The sequence's power is exactly the sum: A ranking between whole and parts does not establish an additive measurement.
